newsitem.title: USA: Ind. legislature passes budget, no accord on arena.
newsitem.headline: Ind. legislature passes budget, no accord on arena.

text.p: Indiana legislators approved a $17.5 billion biennium budget, but failed to address legislation for financing a new Indiana Pacers basketball arena and expansion of the Indianapolis convention center.

State representatives approved the budget late Thursday during a special session called by Gov. Frank O'Bannon, one day after the Senate and a little more than two weeks after they had reached an impasse, spokesmen for legislative leaders said Friday.
A spokesman for O'Bannon was not immediately available to comment on the budget or arena developments.
Lawmakers cut $88 million from the budget before introducing it in the special session, including $67 million from Medicaid, staffers said. It passed without amendment.

Senators approved plans for the arena and convention center during their meeting. But representatives reached another stalemate when House Republicans refused to consider enabling legislation for the arena after Democrats sought to tack on an amendment increasing workers compensation benefits.
"In the eleventh hour, really the thirteenth hour, it's a pretty big deal," said Roger Schmelzer, chief legal counsel to House Republican Leader Paul Mannweiler, R-Indianapolis.
But Judson Kring, spokesman for House Speaker John Gregg, D-Sandborn, said the workers compensation amendment would provide a needed boost in benefits for injured workers.
Representatives have scheduled another meeting for May 27 to consider those plans.

The estimated $175 million basketball arena would be financed in part with $50 million of bonds backed by sales and income taxes from a new professional sports development district in downtown Indianapolis that needs legislative approval.

The convention center expansion would be financed through $40 million of bonds backed partly by increases in the hotel/motel tax, rental car tax and a broader application of the ticket tax. All three taxes need legislative approval and Indianapolis City Council backing.
Lawmakers approved the convention center plans during the regular session, but O'Bannon vetoed the bills when they failed to reach a budget agreement.
